title: Trump Urges Calls to Cotton in Push for Permanent Daylight Saving Time
summary:
On Saturday, October 3, President Donald Trump urged Americans to contact Arkansas Senator Tom Cotton to support a bill making daylight saving time permanent. Cotton repeated his opposition, bringing renewed attention to a policy question that affects school travel and the timing of daylight.

During daylight saving time, clocks in most parts of the United States are set one hour ahead of standard time from spring to fall. The current system generally involves changing clocks twice a year. Not every state observes daylight saving time.

The Sunshine Protection Act passed the House of Representatives in July, but opposition in the Senate remains an obstacle. Passage in one chamber of Congress does not mean a proposal has become law. Under this bill, states could opt out if their legislatures acted before its enactment.

Supporters, including the White House, argue that keeping daylight saving time would provide more daylight during hours when Americans are most active. Trump has emphasized the inconvenience of adjusting clocks and the value of evening daylight for activities such as golf and tennis.

Opponents focus on winter mornings. Keeping clocks ahead throughout the year would produce later sunrises by the clock. Cotton says this could leave children traveling to school in darkness. Other critics raise concerns about children waiting for school buses and parents driving to work.

Trump blamed Cotton for blocking the proposal. Cotton repeated his position in a social media post. He said Congress had previously tried permanent daylight saving time and later reversed course after Americans experienced late winter sunrises. He is among several Republican senators opposing the change.

A 2025 Associated Press-NORC poll found that 12 percent of American adults favored the current clock-changing system, 47 percent opposed it and 40 percent were neutral. If required to choose, most preferred keeping the extra hour of evening daylight.

The debate asks lawmakers to weigh convenience and evening activities against the effects of darker winter mornings.
why_it_matters: A permanent clock setting would affect the timing of daylight for school travel, work trips and evening activities.
